structure.title: Act I, scenes 1–4 · A shipwreck and two households in mourning
structure.text: Viola comes ashore believing her brother lost. Olivia mourns her own brother and dismisses Orsino's suitors. Disguised as the boy Cesario, Viola takes a paid position carrying one household's desire into the other.

structure.title: Act I, scene 5 – Act III · A messenger becomes the attraction
structure.text: Viola speaks so well for her employer that Olivia takes an interest in the messenger. Elsewhere in the house a forged letter gives the steward Malvolio every reason he ever wanted for believing his mistress in love with him.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · The twins' paths converge
structure.text: Sebastian, Viola's twin, reaches the same town. Strangers now offer him arguments, friendship and affection earned by somebody else. The public work of sorting out identities involves private feelings that cannot simply change direction on command.

people.name: Viola
people.text: Her paid task is to argue a case she has private reasons for wanting to lose. She can tell Orsino a good deal about her feelings if he will accept that she is telling a story about somebody else.

people.name: Maria and Malvolio
people.role: Maid and steward in Olivia's house
people.text: Both understand the workings of a great household. Maria's talent for imitating a hand exploits Malvolio's pleasure in imagining the authority he would have as Olivia's husband.

context.title: Service gives access
context.text: A messenger may have a private audience with someone an unwanted suitor cannot approach. A servant can handle a letter and know a mistress's handwriting. Rank opens particular doors even as it keeps others closed.

notice.text: What does Malvolio have to work out for himself?
notice.why: The letter leaves some things obscure. The funniest and most painful parts of the reading are the leaps he supplies because he wants the message to be meant for him.

notice.text: When does the joke get an exit?
notice.why: Some people can go back to their ordinary lives as soon as a disguise comes off. Someone persuaded that he is mad has much less power to announce that the fun is over.

opening: Viola survives a shipwreck, disguises herself as a young man, and takes work carrying love messages for a duke. She falls for her employer; the woman receiving his messages falls for her. Nobody can speak plainly without endangering something, and everybody has a persuasive account of their own feelings. Shakespeare surrounds this triangle with drinking, music, vanity, and a practical joke that stops being harmless. Desire makes the characters inventive, while the audience enjoys the precarious privilege of knowing who is actually talking to whom.
